summary: Argues that graphics protocols must handle attention, such as a user pointing at something with a light pen, not just describe images to display. Earlier work in RFC 86, RFC 94 and RFC 125 covered the display side. This note addresses interactive input.

eli5.summary: Showing a picture is only half the job. The other half is knowing when someone touches or points at it. This note says how the network should report that.

questions: what is network graphic attention handling
how should interactive graphics be handled over a network
what types of input devices can graphics systems use
subtitle: How networks should handle user input to graphics displays.

tldr.problem: Previous work on network graphics protocols focused only on sending display data, but interactive graphics systems also need to transmit user input like keyboard presses and light pen touches from the terminal back to the server.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 178 defines attention handling as the process of detecting hardware input, processing its meaning, and transmitting it. A network protocol for attention data must include device identification, data identification, and the data itself.
tldr.outcome: The RFC establishes guidelines for a general attention protocol that can accommodate any type of input device, from simple buttons to complex light pens with position tracking.

facts.label: Protocol elements
facts.value: Device ID, data ID, and data field

facts.label: Light pen output types
facts.value: Memory address, X/Y position, or item ID

today: RFC 178 is a foundational reference for network graphics protocols. While the specific attention protocol was never formally standardized, the architecture and device classification influenced later graphics standards like X11 and modern web graphics frameworks that also separate input handling from display rendering.

sections.title: The Need for Attention Handling
sections.content:
RFC 178 addresses a critical gap in network graphics protocols. Previous RFCs (86, 94, and 125) focused on displaying graphics over a network, but they did not address how users interact with those graphics. Interactive graphics systems need to transmit user input, such as keyboard presses or light pen touches, from the terminal back to the serving host.

The RFC defines attention handling as the process of detecting and servicing user inputs to a graphics system. An attention event is a stimulus from the user, such as a keystroke or light pen usage. The emphasis is on immediate handling—detecting the input, processing it quickly, and either acting on it locally or transmitting it to the application program.
sections.eli5: When someone clicks a light pen or presses a key while looking at a network graphics display, the system needs to notice right away and tell the program what happened.

sections.title: Attention Input Devices
sections.content:
RFC 178 surveys the types of graphics input devices and categorizes them by the information they provide. Pushbuttons and keyboards report a key code and an implicit indication that a keystroke occurred. Analog devices like mice, trackballs, and shaft encoders produce continuous digital values representing rotational position. Tablets capture (X, Y) coordinates on a flat surface, or sometimes (X, Y, Z) for three-dimensional input. Light pens detect beam position or display list location and can even identify the specific image being touched. Internal attentions, like screen overflow or programmed traps, arise from the terminal itself rather than the operator. Logical attentions are software-generated stimuli simulating any of the above.

Intelligent terminals with programmable logic can process attention data locally, reducing network traffic but raising the risk of the display and application getting out of sync if local processing is not properly coordinated.
sections.eli5: Different devices send different kinds of information: a key sends a character, a mouse sends position changes, a light pen sends where it touched, and smart terminals can even combine many inputs into one message.

sections.title: Protocol Structure
sections.content:
RFC 178 proposes a three-part structure for a network attention protocol. The device identification field uniquely identifies the type of input device, distinguishing between device classes (buttons, tablets, light pens) and even different logical modes of the same device. The RFC notes that a device table should be maintained in the network, possibly at each host supporting graphics applications.

The data identification field describes what follows: the number of data units, qualitative description (character code, coordinates, memory address, item name), and format information. Finally, the data field contains the actual input, which may be of arbitrary length and organization. This general framework accommodates any current or future input device without requiring protocol changes.
sections.eli5: The message has three parts: which device sent it, what kind of information it contains, and the actual information itself. This way, any device can talk to the network.

sections.title: System Configurations
sections.content:
The RFC discusses how attention handling fits into different graphics system architectures. In a stand-alone configuration, the application program is device-dependent, handling both graphics display and input processing. With standardized formats, input and output processors are separated from the application, allowing the same program to work with different devices. In a network configuration, the application, input processor, and output processor may reside on different hosts; standardized formats become network standards.

Intelligent terminals can perform local attention processing, but this introduces complexity: the terminal's local data structure and the server's application state must stay synchronized. A more expressive protocol is needed to communicate these local changes back to the serving host.
sections.eli5: The simplest setup has everything in one machine. The next step puts the device handlers in separate software. Over a network, they can be on different computers. Smart terminals add another layer by doing some processing locally.
